source.title: TPV: Parameter Perturbations Through the Lens of Test Prediction Variance

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, including appendices. It contains some flattened figure text, but the relevant result descriptions are also stated in prose.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures how width, training-set size, and regularization relate to test loss and TPV, using methods different from the claim versions’ specified experiments. Its results do not test random-label memorization, the specified architecture comparisons, optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout’s direct effect on test error, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported width and regularization results bearing on generalization, plus the reported TPV stability and training-set-size conditions. The paper’s pruning-method comparisons and model-selection applications are not rows: they evaluate the authors’ proposed method rather than the claim’s objects. Cited prior-work findings are excluded.
record.test_reason: The dropout sweep measures held-out cross-entropy as dropout strength changes, including a zero-dropout baseline, and explicitly reports improvement followed by underfitting. This tests V6 in CIFAR-10 MLPs. The width sweeps report lower test loss but do not establish widening beyond the width needed to fit the training data, so they cannot establish V2's defining condition.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors present TPV as a local post-training perturbation measure, derive a common geometry–covariance trace framework, and argue that training-set TPV can estimate test-set TPV. They report broader empirical stability than their theorem guarantees, failures with very small training sets or large perturbations, and a training-loss-dependent relationship with clean test loss. They also demonstrate pruning and model-selection applications.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies local prediction variance under post-training perturbations and its relation to test loss, using synthetic regression, pretrained image classifiers, and regularization sweeps. It does not reproduce the specified original experiments on random-label memorization, architecture, optimizers, batch size, or magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.method_sensitivity: TPV stability changes with training-set size and perturbation magnitude; the TPV/test-loss relation changes between low- and high-training-loss regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: Test loss decreases with width in synthetic MLPs and pretrained MobileNetV2 comparisons, without establishing the interpolation threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider networks can have lower held-out loss in synthetic regression and pretrained image-classifier comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Training-set and test-set TPV often agree across widths and generalization gaps, with failures at very small sample sizes or large perturbations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Local prediction-variance estimates can transfer from training inputs to test inputs under sample-size and perturbation conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: TPV and clean test loss correlate positively at low training loss, while underfitting can invert the relationship.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The usefulness of label-noise TPV as a test-loss proxy depends on the training-loss regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Jacobian-curvature trace ranks label-noise sensitivity in the opposite direction in the reported weight-decay sweep.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled Jacobian-curvature trace need not predict robustness to subsequent noisy-logit fine-tuning.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The text gives no numerical per-width results for the relevant trend statements. The synthetic-width result is reported in prose, and several comparisons are described through figures. The TPV stability theorem relies on overparameterization and isotropic perturbation assumptions; the empirical result is stated to break for small training sets or large perturbations. The width comparisons do not establish zero training error at every width.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise eligible width, regularization, or TPV stability findings were omitted. Detailed pruning-baseline accuracy/compression curves and deployment model-selection results are excluded because they evaluate the proposed pruning/model-selection applications, not a version’s named outcome.

untested.parts: No paired natural-label and fixed random-label experiments measuring training fit and chance-level held-out accuracy.
Whether test error keeps falling after the width needed for zero training error; the interpolation threshold and training-to-convergence condition are not established.
No controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparison, local-connectivity intervention, or convolutional initialization experiment.
No reported held-out optimizer comparison under a defined tuning budget. The preliminary SGD/Adam discussion reports a training-loss difference, without comparative held-out results.
No large-batch held-out performance comparison under fixed epoch budgets or adapted recipes.
Classification error rates, convolutional dropout-only effects, very small training sets, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with data augmentation are not established.
No magnitude-aware sharpness ranking of generalization gaps among comparably fitted convolutional networks, or comparison with norm and margin measures.
No identification and removal of memorized examples followed by retraining against random-removal controls.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any version. Different architectures or datasets alone do not justify limits_scope. The missing interpolation condition prevents a V2 verdict; it is an untested condition, not evidence against V2. V6 evidence is qualitative held-out cross-entropy evidence from separately trained dropout settings, with one reference-model training run per setting.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out performance.

The width results use a three-layer MLP on synthetic data and pretrained MobileNetV2 models on CIFAR-10/100, not one-hidden-layer ReLU networks trained to convergence on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10. The text does not establish zero training error at each width or sweep past the interpolation threshold.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks trained from scratch, local connectivity, learned sparse connections, or convolutional initialization.
No controlled comparison of adaptive optimizers against SGD/momentum on held-out performance.
No large-batch versus small-batch generalization comparison under fixed epoch budgets or adapted recipes.

Dropout is varied as a regularizer in TPV/test-loss correlation experiments, but the paper does not report the specified dropout-versus-no-dropout test-error comparison or the very-small-training-set condition.

The study does not test magnitude-aware sharpness or rank generalization gaps among similarly low-training-loss networks. Its TPV stability result concerns train/test TPV agreement, and its sharpness comparison concerns label-noise sensitivity.
No memorized training examples are identified, removed, or compared with random removals.

rows.measure: test loss in relation to TPV
rows.value: Dropout exhibits the same U-shaped relationship: test loss decreases with TPV in the low-training-loss regime, then rises as TPV falls further in the high-training-loss regime.
rows.note: This is a TPV/test-loss relationship across regularization settings, not a direct estimate of dropout’s effect versus no dropout.
rows.check: The record incorrectly excludes this from V6. Reference models are trained separately at dropout probabilities including zero, and their clean held-out cross-entropy is measured. Appendix G.3.2 explicitly reports decreasing test loss with increasing dropout in the low-training-loss regime, followed by underfitting. Separate the beneficial and excessive-dropout conditions; exact probabilities at the transition are not recoverable from the supplied flattened figure.
